entries.title: No relief from the heat as September kicks off. Is this normal?
entries.summary: <p>September 1 was the start of meteorological Fall — but also the start of yet another heat wave in the Chicago area. A heat advisory was issued by Chicago's Office of Emergency Management and Communications for "dangerous heat" on Tuesday. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/31/temperature-heat-forecast" target="_blank" ><u>Peak heat indices</u></a> — or how the temperature feels — were expected to reach 100 to 105 degrees on Tuesday and Wednesday due to humidity. Even higher heat indices were possible south of Interstate 80, National Weather Service Chicago said on X.</p><h3>Is it unusual for September to be so hot?</h3><p>This week’s high temperatures — the result of a heat dome moving into the area — will keep temperatures about 10 degrees above the normal average for late August and early September, said Zachary Yack, meteorologist at the National Weather Service Romeoville in a Sun-Times article by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/31/temperature-heat-forecast" target="_blank" ><u>David Struett</u></a>.</p><p>This heat wave is “somewhat unusual and a significant and potentially dangerous late-season event,” said Dr. Ashish Sharma, Climate and Urban Sustainability Lead at Discovery Partners Institute at University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. “Chicago’s normal high in this period is about 80 degrees.”</p><p>But hot Septembers are not new. Back in 2015, the National Weather Service answered the question “<a class="Link" href="https://www.weather.gov/ilx/sep2015-heat" target="_blank" ><u>How Unusual is this September Heat Wave</u></a>?”</p><p>The answer: Not that unusual.</p><p>“Looking back at the climate statistics since 1980, there have generally been about 3 days per September with highs of at least 90 degrees. This does not happen every year, but is somewhat regular,” the NWS wrote in 2015.</p><h3>Does it feel hotter because it’s been such a hot summer?</h3><p>Maybe. In July, Chicago had two heat waves when temperatures topped 90 degrees.</p><p>“There is probably some heat fatigue for Chicagoans. Many of us are mentally and physically tired of it,” said Sharma.</p><p>“Chicago’s July was warmer than normal. This late burst of heat adds to an already demanding summer, especially when people were looking for more pleasant weather in September after schools are reopened,” said Sharma.</p><p>The heat has taken a severe toll. In August, Cook County recorded its 13th <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/20/cook-county-records-13th-heat-death-of-2026-more-than-doubling-previous-decade-high" target="_blank" ><u>heat death</u></a> of the year.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/extreme-heat-wave-death-chicago-cook-county-oak-lawn-july-stroke-stress-elderly-air-conditioning" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ and Chicago Sun-Times analysis</u></a> of medical examiner data previously found Cook County has had more deaths related to the heat in 2026 than any other year in the last decade. Heat deaths previously peaked in Cook County in 2019 and 2022 when there were six deaths each.</p><h3>Does it feel hotter because it’s humid?</h3><p>Yes. And maybe because of corn.</p><p>“When the air contains a great deal of moisture, sweat cannot evaporate as efficiently, and evaporation is the body’s primary cooling mechanism. That is why an air temperature in the mid-90s can produce a heat index near 105 degrees, and locally close to 110,” said Sharma.</p><p>“The National Weather Service also points to moisture moving into the region and evapotranspiration from crops, sometimes called ‘corn sweat,’ as contributors to the high humidity,” he added.</p><h3>Does it feel hotter because the weather has been more extreme this summer?</h3><p>Maybe. This summer, the Chicago area has been pummeled by heat waves, tornadoes, storms, flooding and wildfire smoke.</p><p>As of the end of August, 207 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/27/200-tornadoes-illinois-2026" target="_blank" ><u>tornadoes</u></a> and counting have touched down in Illinois this year, reported WBEZ/Grist reporter JuanPablo Ramirez-Franco.</p><p>The previous record of 142 funnel clouds was set just two years ago, according to Trent Ford, the Illinois state climatologist. This is the third year in a row that Illinois has experienced a triple-digit tornado season; the state’s historical average is closer to <a class="Link" href="https://stateclimatologist.isws.illinois.edu/climate-of-illinois/tornadoes-in-illinois/" target="_blank" ><u>50</u></a>.</p><p>The Chicago area has also seen some of the most severe storms in recent memory this summer, which have caused damage to homes, widespread flooding and, for the first time, nearly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/06/chicago-deep-tunnel-historic-flooding-tarp-reservoir-weather-climate-change" target="_blank" ><u>filled the reservoirs</u></a> meant to manage stormwater and flooding, reported Sun-Times reporter Mary Norkol.</p><p></p><p>If anyone is craving fall sweater weather, they will have to grab some sunscreen instead.</p>

entries.title: White Sox prospect Tanner McDougal looking to show improved mechanics after rocky debut
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON – White Sox right-hander <b>Tanner McDougal</b>’s major league debut on Aug. 13 was the realization of a lifelong dream, both for him and his father Mike, who pitched for six professional seasons but topped out in Triple-A.</p><p>It also saw him walk three batters and plunk another to force in a run, prompting the ballyhooed prospect’s return to Charlotte for the following two and a half weeks.</p><p>“It sucked, but I felt like I got over it relatively quick compared to other ways I could have handled the situation,” said McDougal, who felt his return to the minors was a necessary reset. “Talked to <b>Davis [Martin]</b> a little bit when he was rehabbing down in Charlotte. He kind of gave me some good insight on when he struggled, when it feels like it’s speeding up on him, what he does about it. That helps me a lot.”</p><p>Ever since McDougal went down with a flexor strain at the end of April, there’s been a frenzied nature to his season. The 23-year-old felt the arm injury itself stemmed from trying to compensate in his delivery for the hamstring tightness he experienced the outing before it.</p><p>The White Sox moved him to relief with the view that there wasn’t enough time left in the season to build McDougal up to starting again and still have him help the major league team. And McDougal feels his erratic control and performance, still on display as he walked six and allowed seven earned runs in 4 ⅔ innings in Triple-A in between big league call-ups, has come from still-lingering bad mechanical habits that have yet to be fully ironed out.</p><p>He sees progress, even if the minor league results don’t show it yet.</p><p>“Over the past few weeks I’ve gotten back to what is normal,” McDougal said. “Just try to stay through the ball as long as possible. I think I’ve been a little peel-y this year, peeling off pitches late, which is causing stuff to run back over the middle.”</p><p>The concept of McDougal at his best, which offers high-90s velocity and a slider that racked up massive miss rates in Double-A last year, sounds like a late-inning bullpen weapon. It also sounds like he’ll have to prove his way into such a role.</p><p>“He’s going to be part of our future here, whether that’s near-term or long-term,” said manager Will Venable. “He’s a guy we are really excited about.”</p><p><b>Montgomery ready for home stretch</b></p><p>Even though he finished it by launching his 50th career home run on Monday, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/25/white-sox-shortstop-colson-montgomery-offensive-struggles-jake-burger-will-venable-derek-shomon-jacob-degrom-all-star-home-runs" target="_blank" ><b><u>Colson Montgomery</u></b><u> had an August to forget</u></a>, batting .200/.277/.360 and striking out in a whopping 42% of his plate appearances.</p><p>Nevertheless, he ended the month feeling confident in his plate approach, and what it needs to look like going forward.</p><p>“I'm going to take my walks, and then if you throw a ball over the plate, I'm probably going to do some damage on it,” Montgomery said. “You want to do it consistently and it's really hard to, but I feel good."</p><p><b>Martin set to return</b></p><p>It won’t be official until the White Sox can reveal the corresponding roster move, but Martin is expected to be activated off the injured list to start Wednesday’s game.</p>

entries.title: Tommy Pham looking to 'prove everyone wrong' in late-season reunion with White Sox
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — Tommy Pham warmly praised the communication he had with Phillies general manager Preston Mattingly before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/31/tyler-schweitzer-tyler-gilbert-white-sox-davis-martin-will-venable-kyle-teel-ryan-fuller-astros-series-houston" target="_blank" ><u>he was traded to the White Sox for cash</u></a> on Monday.</p><p>That compliment makes sense in light of the ultimatum the 38-year-old outfielder issued from Triple-A Lehigh Valley.</p><p>“I wanted to give the Phillies a heads up that that was my last week in Triple-A,” Pham said after taking batting practice with his new team on Tuesday. “I checked out. Being in the situation I'm in, a guy with 10-plus [years of MLB service time] playing Triple-A like that, I was over it.”</p><p>As Pham noted, it showed with a 1-for-25 finish to his IronPigs tenure. Nevertheless, Mattingly told him that multiple teams were interested in swinging a trade for him in light of the .288/.420/.455 line Pham had in Lehigh Valley before his fade, and he was heartened to hear the White Sox were pushing for a reunion.</p><p>A player who is notably cognizant and forthright about how his intense approach to the sport is perceived, and how his performance is measured, Pham views an opportunity to contribute to a playoff hopeful Sox team down the stretch as a chance to rebuke how he’s often evaluated on multiple fronts.</p><p>“Everyone says on Twitter I'm a clubhouse cancer,” Pham quipped when asked about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/31/white-sox-manager-will-venable-excited-to-bring-tommy-pham-jordan-leasure-mike-vasil-jose-urquidy-chris-getz-jake-cave-tyler-schweitzer-brenton-doyle-everson-pereira" target="_blank" ><u>the Sox coveting the veteran edge he’ll bring to their young roster</u></a>. “The only thing I can do is have some success to prove everyone wrong. It will say a lot individually if I help the team win and make the postseason roster. It will say a lot to how bad our CBA [collective bargaining agreement] is right now and how it's hurting players like me. That's something that the fans don't really understand.”</p><p>The White Sox are not an exception to Pham’s description of a league obsessed with stockpiling cheap, young players over proven veterans. But this Sox front office cast themselves as team that prioritizes makeup in player evaluation more than the average club, view it as part of their surprising success, and have now acquired Pham two separate times to influence two very different teams.</p><p>“We've seen more guys outperform probably what the initial expectations were coming into the year, and we feel like [makeup is] a big part of it,” Sox assistant general manager Josh Barfield told the Sun-Times. “That's why we've been able to stay away from some of the prolonged struggles.”</p><p>Having played roughly .500 ball since an 18-10 May, the Sox entering September with a three-game lead in the American League Central can be attested to showing the resilience to avoid long slumps, even if opinions can differ as to how they’ve pulled it off.</p><p>“Mindset really doesn't really factor on wins and losses,” said Sam Antonacci, of all people. “Honestly, it’s who's just the better group of players out there, and fortunately, we've been the better group of players for more times than not.”</p><p>Does Pham, as second right-handed platoon bat, improve the White Sox player group? Time will tell, but it might make them a more aggressively deployed group, even with a manager who already pinch-hits at the third-highest rate in MLB.</p><p>“A day where we have [Randal Grichuk] and Tommy on the bench, you have multiple moves you feel good about,” said Will Venable. “Maybe not as much earlier in the game, but having another move later in the game, I think certainly opens up some stuff.”</p><p>So if Pham has a memorable impact in the final month for the 2026 White Sox, a likely route is via late-game heroics that have playoff implications. For someone who was around for the historically awful 2024 Sox season, and was considering asking for his release and going home a week ago, that would be quite a flip.</p><p>“It just shows you how quick things can turn around,” Pham said. “Especially in the AL Central.”</p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: ‘Foodie’ and World Series vet Kevin Gausman sees something cooking in Cubs: ‘The recipe is kind of there’
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> starting pitcher <b>Kevin Gausman</b> knows a thing or two about food. And he’d like to know more.</p><p>“Chicago, I need your help,” he tweeted Monday. “Trying to figure out who has the best cinnamon rolls in the city!”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Chicago I need your help. Trying to figure out who has the best cinnamon rolls in the city! <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/LetMeKnow?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#LetMeKnow</a></p>— Kevin Gausman (@KevinGausman) <a href="https://x.com/KevinGausman/status/2094433157734900218?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 31, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The post got hundreds of responses, many pointing Gausman toward Ann Sather, a staple of the North Side.</p><p>“I just like good food,” he told Marquee Sports Network, which set him up with an Ann Sather taste test.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Kevin Gausman asked Chicagoans for the best cinnamon rolls in the city, so we HAD to bring him Ann Sather's 😍<br><br>Here's how he rated it ⬇️ <a href="https://t.co/Oj0cql54D9">pic.twitter.com/Oj0cql54D9</a></p>— Marquee Sports Network (@WatchMarquee) <a href="https://x.com/WatchMarquee/status/2094557091444707598?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 31, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Maybe that’s why he kept talking in culinary terms when describing something else he likes: the Cubs’ chances in the postseason in October.</p><p>“The biggest thing with teams that make it to the World Series is you have to have a really good defense, you have to have good pitching, and you have to have timely hitting,” Gausman said Tuesday. “We pretty much have just about all of that. Time will tell, obviously. But the recipe is kind of there.”</p><p>The cooks in the Cubs’ kitchen have indeed whipped up a contender. They started September with the highest-scoring offense in baseball, the best defensive squad in the game and — although team president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/01/cubs-home-runs-record-jed-hoyer-front-office-pitching-starting-rotation-playoffs-postseason-shota-imanaga-matthew-boyd" target="_blank" >wants more from his pitching staff</a> — a couple of recently acquired hurlers in Gausman and fellow right-hander <b>Clay Holmes</b>, who look capable of delivering in the playoffs.</p><p>Gausman, who referred to himself as a “foodie” during his cinnamon-roll tasting, is an expert on more than just sweet treats. He <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/08/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-world-series-blue-jays-yankees-dodgers" target="_blank" >pitched in the World Series last fall</a>, logging 12 ‰ innings in two starts with the Blue Jays, who came agonizingly close to dethroning the Dodgers. He also played a big role in the Jays’ run overall, pitching in six playoff games with a 2.93 ERA.</p><p>So he knows what these Cubs need to do to thrive.</p><p>“It’s just about putting it all together and not letting those moments get too big,” Gausman said. “There are going to be moments where it’s going to get pretty big and it’s going to get pretty crazy, and if you’re not prepared for it, it’ll hit you right in the face.</p><p>“We’ve got a lot of guys who’ve played in the postseason and know that it’s all about how much you can control your emotions and your heartbeat.”</p><p>Wait a minute — that didn’t have anything to do with food. Can we get back on topic here and say something meatier about these Cubs?</p><p>“The No. 1 thing is they’re hungry. They’re hungry for success,” Gausman said. “They want it for this team, they want it for this fan base, and they want it for each other. And they expect to win every day.</p><p>“I’ve only been on a couple teams that felt that way, and when you have the talent to do it, mixed with that mentality, it can be pretty fun to be around.”</p><p>Chef’s kiss.</p><h3>Swanson swinging</h3><p>Injured shortstop <b>Dansby Swanson</b> started taking swings Monday as he works back from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/17/cubs-injuries-dansby-swanson-oblique-edward-cabrera-blister-nico-hoerner-pedro-ramizrez-craig-counsell-david-peterson-javier-assad-rotation-bullpen" target="_blank" >a strained oblique</a>.</p><p>“We’re making progress,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Tuesday. “With an oblique, the swinging is the thing that we have to go slowly with and kind of repeat days. But [Monday] was a good day on his first day swinging. We’re along the timeline that we’d hoped. We just can’t skip any steps and [will] continue on the same path that we’re on.”</p><h3>Steele standing</h3><p>Left-handed starter <b>Justin Steele</b> will begin a rehab assignment with Triple-A Iowa on Wednesday. He hasn’t pitched since April of last season while recovering from major elbow surgery and a setback earlier this year.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 entries.title: Battle intensifies over Emanuel Congregation's new lakefront home in Edgewater
entries.summary: <p>A proposal to transform Emanuel Congregation’s lakefront property in Edgewater into a mixed-use development with a new synagogue has sparked a battle between neighborhood groups and Friends of the Parks have now joined the fray.</p><p>Emanuel announced last year that it would partner with Chicago-based developer Fern Hill to build a synagogue at its current location, 5959 N. Sheridan Road. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/05/15/edgewater-synagogue-emanuel-updated-project-plans-3-lakefront-towers" >latest plans</a> show the site would include three towers, with retail and an estimated 600 units of housing, including affordable.</p><p>The congregation will own its portion of the project, and it's not paying for the construction. Instead, it’s giving the land for free to Fern Hill, who will pay for and oversee the development, alongside two additional parcels the developer purchased.</p><p>Many consider the site as the only developable lakefront property left in Edgewater and housing advocates said Edgewater desperately needs more housing, as it becomes an increasingly attractive neighborhood for renters. But some residents and local businesses fiercely oppose Emanuel's project, calling for lakefront protections. Friends of the Parks joined their call earlier this month.</p><p>The groups came head-to-head Sunday when the Edgewater Residents for Responsible Development held its "Rally for our Lakefront" to oppose Emanuel and Fern Hill's project. The rally was held at the intersection of Thorndale Avenue and Sheridan Road, near the synagogue, and drew a counterprotest that included members of the Jewish Council of Urban Affairs and Neighbors of Edgewater and Uptown, who support the project for its family-sized and affordable units.</p><p>Emanuel didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Chicago Department of Planning and Development Deputy Commissioner Peter Strazzabosco said the agency doesn't anticipate the project will be heard during the Plan Commission's September meeting.</p><p>The ERRD said it represents more than 600 Edgewater residents and small businesses. Its president, Patricia Sharkey, said the rally came together because they felt it was shut out of conversations about the project by Ald. Leni Manaa-Hoppenworth (48th).</p><p>Sharkey said they support affordable housing, but it doesn’t believe Emanuel's site is the right place. In June, the group issued a call for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/04/edgewater-residents-emanuel-congregation-land-public-park" >Chicago Park District to purchase the site</a> to "complete the lakefront park system" and convert it into a park, saying the synagogue could move to another location. </p><p>The ERRD believes the property falls under the city's Lakefront Protection Ordinance. The ordinance says an appropriate public agency — like the park district — should “acquire such properties or rights as may be necessary and desirable” along the lakefront. </p><p>“If this goes the wrong way, if the Plan Commission and our alderwoman and [the] congregation don't wake up to this … they will be making the Lakefront Protection Ordinance into something that's simply toothless, that has no meaning,” Sharkey said.</p><p>The park district said that it's "in communication with the Alderwoman, who indicates that she supports the community benefits associated with [the] current proposal. Any acquisition would require significant resources and funding. The District will continue to assess all opportunities related to acquiring and developing future, public parkland at the Edgewater site.”</p><p>In July, Manaa-Hoppenworth allowed Fern Hill’s proposal to move forward because the developer agreed to key changes, including more family-sized units and guaranteed public access to the lakefront through a public access easement. Under the easement, Fern Hill would provide free, publicly accessible restrooms, storage facilities for nearby beaches and parks, a $100,000 donation for Max Pastin playground improvements and additional donations to promote public safety, including for bike and pedestrian infrastructure.</p><p>But Friends of the Parks wants Fern Hill to also dedicate a strip of the shoreline to the park district, maintain public access to the shoreline during construction and conduct a full environmental and shoreline investigation for the site, among other requests.</p><p>“This is possibly the only chance the public will have to secure the final piece of the city’s northern shoreline. The 1.9-acre lakefront parcels at the center of the proposal sit between two existing public beaches, making this a rare and possibly final opportunity to close the gap,” Brian Gladstein, executive director of Friends of the Park, said in an Aug. 26 news release. “Elected officials need to do what’s right by the people of Chicago and help create more public park space for everyone that’s accessible to all.”</p><p>Manaa-Hoppenworth said in a statement Monday that “the land in question is not undeveloped and not for sale.”</p><p>“There appears to be an attempt to erase the synagogue, its history, and its people from our community by those who oppose building new homes,” she said. “Friends of the Parks was approached by the same anti-housing organization currently suing the city over other pro-housing policy changes, and this is that group’s latest attempt to block new homes being built in Edgewater.”</p><p>Neighbors of Edgewater and Uptown support Emanuel's redevelopment plan. The parcel, two blocks from the Red Line and close to multiple bus routes, is “exactly where Chicago should be building more housing,” Neville Hemming, the nonprofit's president, said in a news release.</p><p></p><p>“Chicago cannot say we have a housing shortage and then fight new homes every time somebody proposes building them,” Hemming said. “If we aren’t willing to add housing two blocks from the Red Line in one of the most walkable neighborhoods in the city, where exactly are we supposed to build it?”</p><p>As of July, Chicago's rent growth was the fourth-fastest among the nation’s 50 largest metropolitan areas, according to Zillow. And the Chicago area is short nearly 225,000 affordable rental units for its poorest residents, according to a 2026 report from the Housing Action Illinois and the National Low Income Housing Coalition.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/04/edgewater-residents-emanuel-congregation-land-public-park" >Group of Edgewater residents want Emanuel Congregation’s land to become public park</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/05/15/edgewater-synagogue-emanuel-updated-project-plans-3-lakefront-towers" >Edgewater synagogue’s updated project plans include 3 lakefront towers</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/30/judge-cohen-dismisses-edgewater-residents-businesses-lawsuit-broadway-upzoning" >Judge dismisses Edgewater residents, businesses’ lawsuit over Broadway zoning changes</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Money isn't everything: With big contract in reach, QB Caleb Williams wants to make sure Bears keep winning
entries.summary: <p>If anyone can play it cool about the possibility of landing a contract worth a quarter of a billion dollars, it’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>. But no matter how focused he is on the immediate, there’s no ignoring what potentially awaits him if he takes another step forward this season.</p><p>He shrugged when asked about it Tuesday. Money doesn’t drive him, he said, though he’s never made money quite like this. And not only would it be a stunning financial windfall, but it would give him and the team long-term stability.</p><p>He’s made quite a bit of money already, including an estimated $10 million in N.I.L. deals in college, his current four-year, $39.5 million rookie contract and various investments. Even as Williams indulged the conversation, he didn’t get dollar signs in his eyes.</p><p>“Money’s not a motivating factor for me in that sense,” he said. “If I wanted to be done today, I’d be fine. If I wanted to be done and go somewhere and disappear for a long time and never come back and y’all would never see me again, I’d be OK. That’s not my motivation.</p><p>“Winning, winning, winning handles everything... so that’s where my mind’s at.”</p><p>Williams is entering the always-pivotal third season for a quarterback, when teams typically gain certainty of what they have. His predecessors, Justin Fields and Mitch Trubisky, were lost causes by then and soon were out of the building. Business as usual for the Bears.</p><p>That’s the part that really speaks to Williams. He never talked about money leading up to the Bears drafting him. He did, though, say he wanted to “create history and rewrite history.” Being the long-awaited answer at quarterback is priceless.</p><p>“I obviously want to be here forever,” Williams said. “That’s a goal of mine: to be at one place until I’m done, until I decide that it’s over for me and I want to go home and ride off into the sun... I’ll be here.”</p><p>A five-year extension, common for quarterbacks at his stage, likely would eliminate the Bears’ fifth-year option for him — their deadline to trigger it is in May — and run through the 2032 season.</p><p>The last time the Bears gave a long-term extension to a quarterback they drafted was more than three decades ago with Jim Harbaugh. But ever since they had the top pick of the 2024 draft in hand, there’s been hope that Williams could be the guy.</p><p>He’ll need to do more to prove that. He set the franchise record for yards passing last season, helped the Bears win their first playoff game in 15 years and delivered jaw-dropping highlights. He also was last in the NFL in completion percentage — he finished at 58.1, well below coach Ben Johnson’s standard of 70% — and 22nd in passer rating.</p><p>If he rounds out his game, the market for his new deal likely would be at least $250 million over five years. Fourteen NFL quarterbacks are on contracts paying at least $44 million per season, and those prices go up every year as the salary cap grows.</p><p>If he wants that much, that is. Williams, who doesn’t have an agent, implied that his priority will be to ensure that his contract doesn’t prevent the Bears from building a championship-caliber roster.</p><p>“The most important thing is being able to make sure when I do get my contract that we can keep winning, that we can keep progressing as a team,” he said. “That’s my biggest goal when those moments do come up, when that time does come up, is how can this help us and propel us?</p><p>“Yes, it’s going to help me, but how can it keep us steady and be able to keep winning games, because that’s most important to me.”</p><p>Maybe that shrug about money was genuine.</p><p>Everyone in the organization seems to believe he’s headed toward a breakout season, which would all but clinch the contract extension, and general manager Ryan Poles and his staff have been factoring it into their salary-cap plans for future seasons.</p><p>Poles and Johnson will be the ones deciding on that commitment, and both sound like they’re already leaning that way. Poles said Tuesday he loves where Williams is at in his development, and Johnson raved about everything from his demeanor to his practice habits and grasp of the offense.</p><p>“He knows what he’s doing,” Johnson said. “He’s executing at a much higher clip than he ever has, and it’s going to continue to grow. He’s going to continue to elevate everyone around him, coaches included.”</p><p>Poles said in February <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/25/new-conversation-bears-gm-ryan-poles-planning-ahead-for-potential-contract-extension-for-qb-caleb-williams" >the Bears were getting “closer and closer to clarity” on Williams’ trajectory</a>, but cautioned that they need to see consistency and added, “He knows he’s got work to do.”</p><p>That work is well underway. Johnson has continued to pepper Williams about footwork and reading defenses. His decisions must be smarter and his passes more accurate. The checklist to be a franchise quarterback is long and the vetting is rigorous. Teams don’t give a quarter of a billion dollars to just anybody.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Illinois suburbs halt Flock use, suspend officers and review policy amid alleged improper use
entries.summary: <p>Several suburban municipalities are reviewing the use of Flock cameras and placing police officers on leave amid a growing epidemic of alleged police abuse of the vast surveillance system.</p><p>Homer Glen announced Monday that it was suspending the use of Flock cameras within its borders "pending final determination of the investigation and review of the Sheriff’s ALPR protocol" after a Will County sheriff’s deputy was placed on administrative leave amid allegations he misused the technology. </p><p>"The Village understands that the investigation has to take its course and remains committed to public safety," it wrote in a <a class="Link" href="https://www.homerglenil.org/m/newsflash/Home/Detail/990" target="_blank" >statement</a> Monday. "However, given the limited information that has been reported to date, and the privacy concerns at issue, the Village has suspended the utilization of Flock ALPR cameras located within the Village of Homer Glen, pending final determination of the investigation and review of the Sheriff’s ALPR protocol."</p><p>West Chicago is also reviewing its use of Flock cameras after officials announced Tuesday that city police officers may performed unauthorized searches between late 2024 and early 2025 using the technology. The Channahon Police Department is also making a similar review after an investigation found that its officers may have also made unauthorized searches. Officers accused of wrongdoing in each case were placed on administrative leave.</p><p>At West Chicago's request, the DuPage County state’s attorney’s office is investigating alongside an internal inquiry into the officer's conduct and a review of the safeguards around use of the system, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://westchicago.org/news/city-of-west-chicago-statement-regarding-flock-camera-system-review/" target="_blank" >statement</a> from the city.</p><p>"[West Chicago] recognizes the broader public concern surrounding the use of automated license plate readers," the city said in a statement. "These tools have provided important public safety benefits, but their use must be balanced with appropriate safeguards, clear policies, meaningful oversight, and accountability."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/27/flock-license-plate-reader-alpr-chicago-suburb" >Flock license plate readers turn Chicago suburbs into ground zero for bitter fight over surveillance</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/flock-license-plate-reader-explainer" >What to know about Flock’s controversial license plate readers</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/20/former-holiday-hills-police-chief-charged-with-making-nearly-300-unauthorized-searches-court-records" >Former Holiday Hills police chief charged with making nearly 300 unauthorized searches: court records</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>They're among dozens of officers who have been accused of misconduct related to the technology in recent months.</p><p>In recent months, a part-time Prairie Grove police officer, who was also serving as top cop in Holiday Hills, was accused of using the system to stalk people he knew through <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/20/former-holiday-hills-police-chief-charged-with-making-nearly-300-unauthorized-searches-court-records" >nearly 250 unauthorized searches of their license plate movements</a>. He now faces multiple felony charges of official misconduct.</p><p>Last month, Frank McGrath, a former sheriff’s deputy in Kenosha County, Wisconsin, was hit with felony charges after an audit revealed he’d used Flock to spy on a co-worker, according to the agency.</p><p>Law enforcement officials say Flock’s system helps crack cases by allowing them to easily pinpoint crime suspects. But for Illinois State Police's nearly 600 license plate readers — which are made and managed by Chicago-based Motorola Solutions — less than 3% of the more than 3 billion vehicles they scanned over the last year were flagged for investigations.</p><p>Additionally, Flock's data from Illinois has been accessed by out-of-state officials monitoring abortions and by federal immigration agents whose coordination with local police is restricted under state law.</p><p>The Illinois secretary of state’s office investigated the Mount Prospect Police Department last summer after its data was accessed by officials in Texas seeking a woman whose family was concerned she had a self-administered abortion. </p><p>The office's subsequent statewide audit of the technology found Flock “did not have proper safeguards in place for data sharing” and that the northwest suburb’s data was accessed in hundreds of immigration-related searches in early 2025.</p><p>Motorola Solutions has since said it cut off the agency’s access to cameras in Illinois and taken steps to ensure state laws aren’t broken. Flock has announced similar measures.</p>

entries.title: Waukegan man sentenced to 19 years for River North, Loop armed robberies
entries.summary: <p>A man was sentenced to 19 years in federal prison for shooting at a security guard while robbing a bank in the Loop and another in River North three years ago, according to the U.S. Attorney’s office for the Northern District of Illinois.</p><p>Jawad Hakeem, a 51-year-old Waukegan resident, pleaded guilty to firearm and robbery charges earlier this year, the office said. He was sentenced to 19 years in federal prison last week.</p><p>On March 3, 2023, Hakeem brandished a gun while robbing a Chase location in River North, prosecutors said. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/3/30/23663196/chance-encounter-arrest-of-man-accused-of-robbing-loop-bank-and-exchanging-gunfire-with-guard" target="_blank" ><u>Six days later</u></a>, he robbed a Fifth Third bank in the Loop.</p><p>On March 9, 2023, Hakeem read employees’ name tags while threatening to kill them unless they gave him $100,000, prosecutors previously said. He grabbed bags full of nearly $24,000 in cash before exchanging gunfire with a security guard. No one was struck or injured.</p><p>He was arrested four days later in Waukegan, after investigators tracked him down with details from an encounter he had with a woman where he told her he was a “sugar daddy” and that he was running for president in 2024, prosecutors said. He gave the woman his phone number, claiming it was “special” and given to him by T-Mobile.</p><p>He later left behind the gun and the gloves from the robbery, along with other items, when he skipped on Woodlawn motel bill.</p>

entries.title: Family of man fatally shot by law enforcement in Gary wants answers in 'unreal' incident
entries.summary: <p>Like many residents in Gary, Kenneth Williams Sr. lost power at his house after a violent storm ripped through his city on Aug. 11.</p><p>He went without power for two weeks but kept working his security job for Armor Security Forces of Crown Point.</p><p>Being an armed security guard wasn’t something new to the 67-year-old Williams.</p><p>“He’s been doing security off and on for 10 to 15 years,” his son, Kenneth Williams Jr., 47, said Tuesday.</p><p>That experience apparently didn’t help late Friday night as the Army and National Guard veteran was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/30/security-guard-fatally-shot-gary-train-station-9-law-enforcement-officers" target="_blank" >shot to death</a> by Gary police and Lake County Indiana sheriff's deputies while working at the Adam Benjamin Jr. Metro Center near City Hall. </p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1BpGSLsEsG/" target="_blank" ><u>video</u></a> live stream shot by citizen journalist Spin Diana of Gary recorded the moment dozens of rounds were fired.</p><p>“I don’t really know why (he was shot), but it seems really odd,” Williams Jr. said. “I’m not exactly sure what happened. The information is kind of vague. But instead of the attention going to the individual that caused the disturbance, the attention went to my father.”</p><p>As Williams’ grieving family waits for answers, the Indiana State Police is conducting the investigation.</p><p>According to the state police, at 10:54 p.m. Friday, six Gary police officers and three county sheriff’s deputies responded to a report of an armed security officer exhibiting “unusual and erratic behavior.”</p><p>In a statement from the ISP, officers attempted to “de-escalate the situation.” However, at 11:20 p.m., a confrontation occurred between the suspect and responding officers, resulting in an exchange of gunfire, police said. </p><p>Williams was pronounced dead at the scene after midnight on Saturday.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> That’s not elderly abuse,” Jessica Cunningham said. “Is the police in their right mind? </p><p>Cunningham said she was out protesting to raise awareness of the incident.</p><p>“Me being one person, like this can count for something,” Cunningham said. “The (police) officials are trying to sweep it under the rug and letting it be known, putting it out there, that's gonna draw eyes on it.”</p><p>Williams Jr. said his father loved being around family.</p><p>“He was a guy that loved family. He loved to hang around with the kids and the grandkids. He was the guy at the cookout. He’s going to be at the barbecue grill. He's going to be playing cards. He's gonna be talking and laughing, just smiling, giving the kids all kinds of sweets and candies. He was the fun person in the group,” Williams Jr. said. </p><p>Williams Jr. said he last spoke to his father days before he died.</p><p>“I don't know the exact date, but it was like maybe like two or three days before he was killed. We had a conversation. He's telling me about the job. He's about to get ready for a shift. We just had a brief conversation; I just told him we'd catch up later,” Williams Jr. said. </p><p>"I never had the opportunity.”</p>

entries.title: Did Trump detain the “worst of the worst” in Chicago last fall?
entries.summary: <p>The immigration agents’ mission was absolutely clear: Ferret out the “worst of the worst” criminals living in the United States without legal status.</p><p>This was the mantra federal officials repeated throughout the 68<b> </b>most intense days of “Operation Midway Blitz,” which began nearly one year ago, on Sept. 8. Hundreds of armed, masked agents from all over the country hit the streets in and around Chicago, detaining thousands as cameras rolled.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-portrait-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">This criminal alien's rap sheet is longer than a CVS receipt. He was found and arrested in Chicago with an active protection order from a prior assault arrest. His prior convictions include driving on a suspended/revoked license, DUI, assault, and domestic battery. <a href="https://t.co/GLUmHqEGLY">pic.twitter.com/GLUmHqEGLY</a></p>— CBP (@CBP) <a href="https://x.com/CBP/status/1987905692863283605?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 10, 2025</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>But a Chicago Sun-Times / WBEZ analysis of<b> </b>data from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shows that the surge of ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers to seize and detain thousands of people they called “criminal illegal aliens” proved less effective in Chicago than the quieter<b> </b>efforts they had taken earlier in the second Trump administration — and since then.</p><p>Nearly month for month, the analysis of detainee data shows, last fall’s campaign to remove the “worst of the worst” was more hype than reality.</p><p>Federal officers had greater success detaining convicted murderers, rapists, other sex offenders and people convicted of serious assault in many months before and after the height of the “blitz” than during it, the analysis shows. And just 15% of the immigrants detained in the Chicago area during the fall campaign had a prior criminal conviction, a steady decline from a high of 50% right after President Donald Trump’s inauguration.</p><p>The high-profile efforts proved particularly<b> </b>effective in at least one area: When a detainee had a prior conviction for a “traffic offense.”</p><p>Federal officers also achieved great success in detaining immigrants with a prior DUI conviction, a crime prioritized by flamboyant <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/12/gregory-bovino-border-patrol-deportation-elcentro-california-blowing-rock-boone-north-carolina-migrants-immigration?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=12122025%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=12122025%20Morning%20Edition+CID_14194dceee40c1980c345381fce1370b&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Gregory%20Bovino%20is%20the%20star%20of%20Trumps%20deportation%20show%20%20we%20traced%20his%20roots&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" ><u>Border Patrol Cmdr.</u><b><u> </u></b><u>Greg Bovino</u></a>, who was 12 when his own father served time for drunkenly crashing his car, killing a 26-year-old woman. The Chicago detainee data didn’t specify whether anyone died or got hurt in each DUI.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-640000" name="html-embed-module-640000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-table" data-src="visualisation/30063762"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30063762/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="table visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>‘</b>It does not make sense’</h3><p>When Trump retook the White House in January 2025, vowing to deport millions of immigrants via aggressive enforcement, he rolled out his campaign mainly in Democratic cities that didn’t vote for him, including Chicago.</p><p>By Sept. 8, and the start of Midway Blitz, his Department of Homeland Security dedicated its surge to a victim of a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/09/08/operation-midway-blitz-katie-abraham-illinois-dhs-kristi-noem-donald-trump" target="_blank" ><u> fatal DUI crash downstate</u></a> caused by an undocumented Guatemalan man. He fled the crash on Jan 19, 2025, that killed Katie Abraham, 20, of Glenview, and Chloe Polzin, 21, of Deerfield, and is currently serving a 30-year prison sentence.</p><p>"This operation will target the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens in Chicago,” DHS said in a news release. “If you come to our country illegally and break our laws, we will hunt you down, arrest you, deport you, and you will never return.”</p><p>But as detentions around Chicago skyrocketed, topping 3,800 over the 68 fall days<b>, </b>roughly 8 of every 10 people held at the ICE processing facility in Broadview or in other Chicago locations had no criminal conviction<b>. </b>Six of the 10<b> </b>had civil immigration violations — like overstaying a visa; the rest have an unspecified criminal charge pending.</p><p>A DHS spokesperson responded to an interview request with a written statement that didn’t address the specific findings and attacked the raw ICE data collected by the nonprofit Deportation Data Project that was the basis for the analysis as “cherry-picked.” The statement also says those stats count crimes just in the U.S. and don’t account for those in other countries.</p><p>“Since Day One, DHS law enforcement has been delivering on President Trump’s promise to the American people to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members, and terrorists,” it read. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is whether or not they are illegally in the U.S. — full stop.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-0b0000" name="html-embed-module-0b0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30064148"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30064148/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>This apparent lack of targeting meshes with what the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights’ top lawyer witnessed on the front lines of arrests and legal defense around Chicago.</p><p>Instead of knocking on specific doors, immigration officers were flooding places where immigrants were known to live or gather, Fred Tsao says.</p><p>“We saw people getting grabbed off the streets, people who were working on yards, or driving Ubers, selling tamales on the street corner or selling flowers,” Tsao says. “They’re getting tackled, they’re getting grabbed, thrown to the ground and beaten … And quite a number of those folks chose not to contest their deportation cases, which means they are separated from their families.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-0d0000" name="image-0d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Federal immigration enforcement agents stopped a group of people to question their citizenship on Nov. 6, 2025 as U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Greg Bovino led a caravan on the Southwest Side. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Regarding DUI convictions, Tsao says, “I don’t want to minimize how serious these offenses are.” But he says, “Is an arrest and detention and deportation proportionate to the seriousness of the offense?”</p><p>The findings are based on analysis of ICE data collected under a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/09/12/immigration-customs-enforcement-ice-arrests-detentions-deportation-trac" target="_blank" ><u>the Deportation Data Project</u></a>, a collective dedicated to transparency in immigration enforcement. The Sun-Times and WBEZ looked at initial detentions logged in the Chicago area and at arrests made in the six-county Chicago metro region between Jan. 20, 2025, and Aug. 5, 2026.</p><p>ICE’s nameless data lists the most serious charge for each immigrant convicted of a crime but provides no details on charges pending when detained. Some highlights:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-989970c1-a306-11f1-b30b-ebd19b581553"><li>The data shows that 11 people with sex assault convictions were detained in October, during the height of the fall 2025 deportation campaign. But federal agents detained 18 immigrants with sexual assault convictions in less time, during the last 11 days of January following Trump's inauguration. They captured 12 more in March.</li></ul><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-989970c2-a306-11f1-b30b-ebd19b581553"><li>During the nine weeks of last fall’s deportation campaign, federal officers booked five convicted killers. Yet they had detained the same number just before in August 2025 and an additional six that May. </li></ul><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-989970c3-a306-11f1-b30b-ebd19b581553"><li>They also detained five convicted sex offenders during those fall weeks — but seven in February 2025, six in July and five in May 2026.</li></ul><p>The situation<b> </b>baffles Esteban Salazar. The suburban building engineer has been victimized by an undocumented immigrant who was charged with pointing a gun at him. Simultaneously, he's horrified that his innocent Mexican-born relatives were grabbed off area streets last fall, detained and then deported.</p><p>Carlos Mavarez Viloria, a Venezuelan migrant, had been arrested several times for theft and possessing crack cocaine before February 2024 when he pulled what Salazar described as a polished black Beretta inside a 7-Eleven Downtown.</p><p>The weapon turned out to be a copycat lighter. But Salazar, a married father of two, braced himself for the real thing. As Mavarez reached into his own pants and headed toward Salazar at the back of the store, threatening to shoot him, Salazar grasped his own licensed handgun.</p><p><b>“</b>So when he pulled a firearm on me, I was already at the back of the store. He was waving it at me. I don't know if he got a glimpse of my firearm, but he ran out,” Salazar says.</p><p>Cook County court records show other charges against Mavarez through May 2026, with mixed outcomes.</p><p>“Why the ‘F’ was he not on the first plane or bus back? My wife's uncle who was here for 20 years. He was held, it's ridiculous,” Salazar says. "It's tough. As a Mexican, as a Latino, I try to understand what our government's doing but it does not make sense."</p><h3>Strategy changes that could explain arrest and detention trends last fall</h3><p>Amid the<b> </b>officers sent to the Chicago area last fall, most from Border Patrol and ICE assignments in a dozen other states, the Trump administration unleashed a bevy of social media posts, extolling arrests of the “worst of the worst.”</p><p>“Operation Midway Blitz is making Illinois SAFE again. DHS law enforcement has made over 1,500 arrests across Illinois including of pedophiles, vicious gang members, and armed robbers,” Homeland Security <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/DHSgov/status/1977881560641638834]]" target="_blank" ><u>posted on X</u></a><b> </b>in mid-October.</p><p>Weeks later, from Border Patrol’s X account: “Another bad guy busted! In Chicago, CBP apprehended this Bulgarian illegal alien with a rap sheet including: domestic battery, aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, rape, failure to register as a sex offender. Happy to have him off the streets!”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Another bad guy busted! In Chicago, CBP apprehended this Bulgarian illegal alien with a rap sheet including: domestic battery, aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, rape, failure to register as a sex offender. Happy to have him off the streets! <a href="https://t.co/9c3SL0I8qV">pic.twitter.com/9c3SL0I8qV</a></p>— CBP (@CBP) <a href="https://x.com/CBP/status/1985806077573664781?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 4, 2025</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>A change in arrest methods in Illinois may help explain the actual low rates of detaining immigrants with serious criminal records. </p><p>Federal officers began 2025 pursuing arrests of undocumented immigrants through 15 government enforcement methods. But between September and November 2025, they logged only four methods. During those months, they reported no arrests under the Criminal Alien Program that tracks when incarcerated immigrants finish their criminal sentences. CAP arrests had accounted for about 10% of arrests between January and September before the Blitz began.</p><p>Then, from Sept. 8 through Nov. 14, the percentage of arrests defined as “collateral” outpaced “targeted” ones — 53% versus 46%. So more people were getting picked up randomly than on purpose. But from Nov. 15 through March 2026, long after the bulk of extra federal officers had left Chicago, targeted arrests eclipsed collateral ones, 72% to 13% (no arrest method was specified for the rest).</p><p>Months before Operation Midway Blitz stormed Chicago, Trump’s new “Border Czar” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/donald-trump/2024/12/09/border-czar-tom-homan-donald-trump-chicago-pritzker-brandon-johnson-immigration" target="_blank" ><u>Tom Homan stood in Portage Park</u></a> in December 2024, vowing to make Chicago ground zero for deportations. A month later, TV's Dr. Phil would ride along with ICE agents in Chicago, questioning detainees on camera.</p><p>January 2025 was a high for detaining immigrants previously convicted of sexual assault especially, and for murder.</p><p>“That was right after the inauguration, continuing into the first couple of weeks in February and then tailing off,” Tsao says. “If there are any arguments for ICE targeting the so-called ‘worst of the worst,’ it would have been in January.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" entries.title: Boy, 15, shot in West Garfield Park
entries.summary: <p>A 15-year-old boy is recovering in good condition at a hospital after someone shot him in the leg outside of a restaurant late Tuesday in West Garfield Park. </p><p>The boy was on the sidewalk in the first block of South Pulaski Road around 11:15 p.m., Chicago police said. Two people were standing nearby when one of them pulled out a gun and shot the boy. </p><p>He was shot on the leg and was taken to Stroger Hospital in good condition, police said. </p><p>No arrests were made. </p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Roommate's unannounced 'all-nighter' had me worried sick
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm a college junior in need of advice. I share an apartment with two other female students, "Wendy" and "Lauren," who roomed together before I met them. Wendy is sweet and easygoing, but she grew up in a rural area and seems very sheltered. For example, she can't swim and thinks that eating shrimp is exotic, but she likes to clog dance and play the mandolin. She has never mentioned having a boyfriend or even dating. We are completely different, but until recently we got along well.</p><p>A few weeks ago, Wendy asked me to go with her to hear a bluegrass band at a club near campus. By 11 p.m., I was ready to leave, so she drove me to our nearby apartment and said she was going back to keep listening to the band. I woke up around 4 a.m. (long after the club had closed) and realized that Wendy hadn't come home. I was freaked out and tried to call her but discovered that she had left her cellphone at the apartment. I went looking for her (in my car) all over campus and anywhere else I thought she might be. I seriously considered calling the police.</p><p>However, when Lauren got home around 8 a.m., she said, "Oh, Wendy has done this before. She probably hooked up with some guy. I should have warned you." Then Wendy rolled in all starry-eyed about this "great guy" she had slept with, who was a stranger she knew only as "Joe."</p><p>Wendy was unapologetic about the distress she had caused me by disappearing and staying out all night. I was exhausted and furious. When she wondered out loud whether "Joe" would be calling her, I snapped, "Why would he? He's probably sober by now." However, I'm now wondering if I am the sheltered one. Am I being judgmental, and was my concern for Wendy's well-being an overreaction? — <i>NERVOUS IN NORTH CAROLINA</i></p><p><b>DEAR NERVOUS:</b> You now know that Wendy is not as unworldly as you originally thought. It is regrettable that you weren't told how well she gets along with other fans of bluegrass, but now you know. You and your roommates should consider making a pact that if you plan to stay out all night, you will inform the others, because your concern was not unfounded. She could have been in any kind of trouble. Luckily, this time she wasn't, and no, you did not overreact.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've been married for almost 40 years to a woman who is verbally abusive. When we went to counseling 30 years ago, she agreed to stop hitting me, which she has mostly adhered to. She still says hurtful things frequently and then laughs them off. What should a man do to leave an abusive wife? Why should I put up with abusive and demeaning behavior anymore? — <i>ABUSED IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR ABUSED:</b> You should not put up with it. Inform your wife that the verbal jabs hurt you as much as the physical blows did. Offer to return to counseling with her so she can learn to treat you with more kindness and respect. In the meantime, consult a lawyer and be prepared to part ways if she continues to believe her abuse is funny.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Obama Center's First Amendment fail
entries.summary: <p>Former President Barack Obama taught University of Chicago law students about the Constitution for <a class="Link" href="https://www.obama.org/about/administration/chicago-where-it-began/" target="_blank" >over a decade</a> before swearing to uphold it. So when I recently visited the otherwise wonderful <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/18/obama-presidential-center-opening-jackson-park" >Obama Presidential Center</a>, it was jarring to see an interactive First Amendment quiz answer its own questions incorrectly.</p><p>The timing is unfortunate. The digital "Our Five Freedoms" display understates protections for speech while the current president rallies against “fake news,” sues publishers that upset him for <a class="Link" href="https://www.citizensforethics.org/reports-investigations/crew-reports/trump-has-filed-lawsuits-and-claims-demanding-over-70-billion-since-second-term-candidacy-announcement/" target="_blank" >billions</a> of dollars and <a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/labeling-dissent-as-terrorism-new-us-domestic-terrorism-priorities-raise-constitutional-alarms-269161" target="_blank" >conflates</a> dissent with terrorism.</p><p>The quiz, which is part of a larger "Democracy 101" exhibit, poses three hypotheticals drawn from court cases and asks visitors to guess whether the First Amendment applies. One <a class="Link" href="https://media.freedom.press/media/documents/IMG_2400.jpeg" target="_blank" >asks</a> whether the Constitution protects reporters publishing rumors without verification. The quiz <a class="Link" href="https://media.freedom.press/media/documents/IMG_2398.jpg" target="_blank" >says</a> the Supreme Court held it doesn’t.</p><p>That’s not true. Under the seminal 1964 case <a class="Link" href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1963/39" target="_blank" >New York Times v. Sullivan</a> and cases that followed, public figures suing over false reporting must prove actual malice, meaning the journalist knew the statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for the truth. Courts have repeatedly <a class="Link" href="https://law.justia.com/cases/illinois/court-of-appeals-first-appellate-district/2008/1060957.html" target="_blank" >said</a> failure to verify rumors doesn’t clear that bar.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-930000" name="module-930000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Even false speech is constitutionally protected. As the Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/united-states-v-alvarez/" target="_blank" >relayed</a> in 2012 while striking down a law against falsely claiming military honors, “The remedy for speech that is false is speech that is true.”</p><p>Although journalists go to great lengths to report accurately with thorough fact-checking, they often publish rumors and unproven claims made by others, as it's newsworthy such statements were made, even if they aren’t true.</p><p>Journalists are allowed to quote and summarize court filings, official proceedings, statements by government officials and more. That’s why you’re able to read what prosecutors say about accused criminals even before the jury has rendered its verdict, or watch commentators on news networks discuss politicians’ claims about their adversaries.</p><p>Even in cases that don’t involve public figures, disseminating rumors is only actionable if they’re false, defamatory and damaging. And even then, the Constitution still applies — it just permits limited recourse. First Amendment jurisprudence might, for example, allow liability for a defamatory statement but limit the damages the plaintiff can recover.</p><p>Another of the quiz's hypotheticals <a class="Link" href="https://media.freedom.press/media/documents/IMG_2396.jpg" target="_blank" >says</a> the Constitution <a class="Link" href="https://media.freedom.press/media/documents/IMG_2397.jpg" target="_blank" >doesn’t </a>protect shouting fire in a crowded theater when there's no fire. That’s probably the most famous First Amendment <a class="Link" href="https://www.theatlantic.com/national/archive/2012/11/its-time-to-stop-using-the-fire-in-a-crowded-theater-quote/264449/" target="_blank" >myth</a> in existence. </p><p>The fallacy was birthed from Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.'s 1919 opinion in <a class="Link" href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/249/47/" target="_blank" >Schenck v. United States</a>, which wasn't even about shouting “fire." The court upheld Charles Schenck’s prosecution for distributing anti-draft leaflets, concluding he presented a “clear and present danger,” which Holmes awkwardly illustrated with the fire hypothetical. </p><p>Holmes' equation of dissent during wartime to stampedes by panicked theatergoers sounds downright <a class="Link" href="https://time.com/7322106/trump-nspm-7-domestic-terrorism/" target="_blank" ><u>Trumpian</u></a>. Fortunately, the line was what lawyers call dicta — an aside with no binding force. </p><p>A half-century later in <a class="Link" href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/395/444/" target="_blank" ><u>Brandenburg v. Ohio</u></a>, the court adopted a more speech-protective standard: Speech can only be punished when directed at inciting imminent lawlessness and likely to result in such a situation.</p><p>That means whether shouting “fire” can be prosecuted depends on the circumstances and the shouter’s intent. Nonetheless, politicians still invoke the example often, generally to make <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2017/08/25/the-minority-leader-who-cried-wolf-in-a/" target="_blank" >bad analogies</a> to justify speech restrictions that come nowhere close to meeting neither the Schenck, nor Brandenburg standards.</p><p>The Obama Center’s quiz miscites a standard that is arguably looser than either, making the claim that speech that “would create an immediate threat to public safety" is unprotected. Censors would have a field day <a class="Link" href="https://freedom.press/the-classifieds/your-kitchen-cabinets-are-a-national-security-threat/" target="_blank" >abusing</a> a “broad, vague generality” like that, as Justice Hugo Black famously cautioned in the <a class="Link" href="https://freedom.press/the-classifieds/the-pentagon-papers/" target="_blank" ><u>Pentagon Papers</u></a> case.</p><h3>Firing off a right answer </h3><p>The quiz's last question is whether the Constitution protects anti-war slogans. It <a class="Link" href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/403/15/" target="_blank" ><u>does</u></a>, of course, and fortunately the exhibit got that right. But one out of three doesn’t cut it.</p><p>I recognize that the Obama Center can’t capture much legal nuance in its tablet-sized quiz. It’s an entry-level explainer for a broad audience, including children. It isn't a treatise. But the errors in the quiz are closer to inversions than oversimplifications and could lead to children thinking that free speech is easily curtailed, priming them to accept censorship as normal and reasonable. That’s a gift to the Trump administration and future anti-speech officials.</p><p>It’s never been more clear that when we give the government an inch to restrict speech, it takes a mile. Obama should know that better than most — the Trump administration intimidates critics and whistleblowers by predictably <a class="Link" href="https://freedom.press/issues/how-obama-administration-laid-groundwork-trumps-coming-crackdown-press/" target="_blank" ><u>building</u></a> on Obama's crackdown on classified leaks, his scuttling of legislation to protect journalist-source confidentiality, as well as legal precedents <a class="Link" href="https://freedom.press/issues/court-guts-reporters-privilege-in-one-of-the-most-significant-press-freedom-cases-in-decades/" target="_blank" ><u>undermining</u></a> that confidentiality that were also established under Obama's presidency.</p><p>Back then Obama could claim he was burdened with weighing free speech against competing national security interests. He can’t anymore — he’s running a museum, not a war room. The Obama Center needs to update the exhibit and explain why our First Amendment errs on the side of protecting even irresponsible speech.</p><p>That’d be “fire,” as the kids say, sometimes in crowded theaters.</p><p><i>Seth Stern is the director of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation and a First Amendment lawyer.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b00000" name="module-b00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Could Pete Crow-Armstrong be a modern-day Willie Mays?
entries.summary: <p>After reading Brian Sandalow's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/29/cubs-star-pete-crow-armstrong-hits-three-home-runs-to-bolster-mvp-case" >story</a> in Sunday's Sun-Times print edition headlined "3 Pete: PCA Homers Thrice," I had a thought. </p><p>Considering the season Pete Crow-Armstrong has been having, one has to wonder if he is the Cubs’ version of <a class="Link" href="https://baseballhall.org/hall-of-famers/mays-willie" target="_blank" >Hall of Famer Willie Mays</a>.</p><p>Both got off to poor starts. Mays went <a class="Link" href="https://www.mlb.com/news/featured/willie-mays-career-timeline" target="_blank" >0-12</a> before he got his first hit, while Crow-Armstrong went <a class="Link" href="https://www.espn.com/mlb/story/_/id/40025435/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-gets-1st-mlb-hit-tiebreaking-home-run" target="_blank" >0-14</a>. Each broke out of their hitting slumps in similar fashion, by hitting home runs.</p><p>Like Mays, Crow-Armstrong plays center field and is one of the best defensive players in the game. In addition, he hits for power and steals bases like the late great Giant.</p><p>Of course, a couple of All-Star seasons does not necessarily mean that Crow-Armstrong will have a Hall of Fame career, and only time will tell. But so far, he reminds me of the “Say Hey Kid,” and the similarities are unmistakable.</p><p><i>Larry Vigon, Jefferson Park</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-980000" name="module-980000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>High-speed train going nowhere fast</h3><p>The O’Hare Flyer dream transit line is very unlikely to be implemented without huge government subsidies. DePaul University's Joseph Schwieterman, a well-informed longtime advocate of public transit and intercity passenger transportation, is spot-on with his concerns about the O’Hare Flyer's viability. The proposed mostly single-track line would be highly vulnerable to a complete stoppage whenever there is a breakdown. Previous similar Loop-O'Hare express concepts could not make the finances work with the available funding and ridership demand, even before the COVID-19 pandemic emptied out Downtown Chicago.</p><p>The recent almost-disappearance of Chicago's already poorly located Greyhound bus station demonstrates that the city and state lack current financial ability to develop big local and intercity transit projects in the Downtown area. On the other hand, preserving the recently freed-up railroad right-of-way properties for potential O'Hare Flyer implementation 50 years from now could be a prudent, inexpensive action for today.</p><p><i>Arthur Christopher Wilson, retired planner, Metra, West Rogers Park</i></p><h3>What a doll </h3><p>I was living in Lemont in 1991 when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/08/27/dolly-parton-corn-maze-woodstock-all-seasons-orchard" >Dolly Parton</a> was starring in a charming movie being filmed in our humble little town. The movie was "Straight Talk," and Lemont was chosen for its iconic streets and buildings. Plus, a railroad track ran smack dab down the middle of town, adding to the ambiance and charm of the place.</p><p>The movie's producers transformed Lemont's historic downtown to resemble a small Arkansas town for part of the movie. The famed Budnik Building, a centerpiece of Lemont since the 1920s, housed the Budnik Drugstore, which hadn't changed much over the many decades it existed.</p><p>I never chased famous people, but when I heard Parton could actually be seen in my little town, I drove the half-mile to all the excitement. As I expected, people milled around, cops were everywhere and traffic was pretty badly stalled in some places. I parked in a safe spot with a good view of the building where the filming was in progress.</p><p>Eventually, Dolly stepped out of the building into the brilliant sunlight, and shielding her eyes with one hand, she waved at her fans with the other. The crowd went wild upon seeing this beautiful little woman who gleamed in spite of the bright sunlight pouring down over all of us. Did she actually look at me? I think she did, because she took the time to turn her gaze to every person standing in the hot sun.</p><p>I drove home thinking, for some unknown reason, that I had been in the presence of someone very special. I kind of felt a glow inside my heart as I drove back home to — what else? — Main Street.</p><p><i>Kathleen Melia, Niles</i></p><h3>Thumbs-up for holding Meta accountable </h3><p>As a Lane Tech College Prep student, I believe social media companies should be held responsible for how their platforms affect young people. That is why I support the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/technology/2026/08/26/meta-illinois-pay-nearly-768-million-multistate-settlement-teen-social-media-addiction" >Meta lawsuit settlement</a> tied to teen social media addiction.</p><p>Social media has become a normal part of growing up. Apps like Instagram and Facebook make it easy to stay connected with friends, discover new interests and see what's happening around us. But there is also a downside that adults don't always understand. Teenagers can spend hours scrolling without realizing how much time has passed. Seeing other people's posts can also create pressure to look or live a certain way.</p><p>I don't think social media itself is bad. The problem is when companies design their platforms to keep people using them for as long as possible without thinking about how it can affect the youth. If a company knows its platform can negatively affect teenagers, it should be held accountable.</p><p>The settlement will not solve every problem with social media, but I believe it is a step in the right direction. Teenagers should still be able to use social media, but companies should be expected to care about their users instead of only focusing on engagement and profit.</p><p>Young people deserve to have a voice in conversations about technology that affects our everyday lives.</p><p><i>Yafet Abebe, Lane Tech College Prep</i></p><h3>Blanche’s blind spot </h3><p>Attorney General Todd Blanche has <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/03/us/politics/blanche-comey-indictment-seashells.html" target="_blank" >justified the prosecution</a> of James Comey for posting a picture of seashells arranged to spell out "86 47." This is the same Blanche who wanted to enter into a <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/05/19/congress/blanche-doesnt-rule-out-j6-payouts-00927704" target="_blank" >settlement agreement</a> that had the potential to make payments to Jan. 6 rioters who yelled "hang Mike Pence." Seashells on a beach spelling out "86 47" do not rise to the level of clear threat that is reached by a mob yelling to hang the vice president in the Capitol, where the vice president was presiding over a session of the Senate.</p><p><i>Alan Rhine, Glenview</i></p>
