entries.title: Mayor's executive order targets companies helping with deportation campaign, bans companies committing abuses
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson signed a wide-ranging executive order Wednesday meant to prevent corporations that carry out corrupt or abusive practices, including inhumanely assisting in aggressive federal deportation campaigns, from doing business with the city.</p><p>Citing an "unprecedented level of corporate corruption” nationally, the three-pronged order prohibits contracts or subcontracts with a company that has committed workplace discrimination, wage theft, or a defined “public integrity violation” in the past five years; requires a company to disclose its diversity demographics, as well as any contracts it has with any other body of government, such as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE); and creates a 12-member Ethical Procurement Standards Task Force.</p><p>“You think about workers' rights, you think about voting rights, you think about the rights of the LGBTQ+ community. All of us are incredibly vulnerable right now. I'm working to do something about it,” Johnson told WBEZ in an interview Tuesday.</p><p>A public integrity violation includes some actions already banned in city code, such as a conviction of bribery. But unlike city code, it would apply to violations adjudicated outside a courtroom. For instance, a finding by a government oversight agency, like an inspector general or auditor, would also be disqualifying.</p><p>Johnson’s team cited Palantir, a data company profiting from contracts with ICE and the war in Gaza, as being among the corporations footing the bill for President Donald Trump’s ballroom under construction at the White House.</p><p>“We're recognizing that these companies may be engaging in corrupt activities, but for a variety of reasons may not be subject to criminal penalties. Nonetheless, we don't want them doing business with the city of Chicago,” said Johnson’s chief strategy officer, Sheila Bedi.</p><p>All current and future contractors and subcontractors will be required to certify that they have not committed a “public integrity violation” in the past five years, and don’t intend to for the length of a contract. The order directs the city’s chief procurement officer to come up with consequences for violating the new rules.</p><p>City code already bans contractors and subcontractors with any conviction involving theft, deceit, hate crimes, perjury, or treason. Those broader crimes don’t appear to be subject to the executive order, meaning they would still require a formal conviction to be disqualifying.</p><p>In response to Trump administration actions, the decree also contains new reporting requirements. Companies will have to disclose whether they hold contracts with other government or law enforcement agencies, which will then be made public. The order was prompted in part by a campaign called “Not With Our Money” that is pushing governments to use their purchasing power to dissuade companies from aiding or being complicit in militarized deportation campaigns.</p><p>“This is a way to say we want to look closely at what you're doing, and if you're doing corrupt things, then we're not going to use taxpayer dollars to support that,” said Dorian Warren, a spokesperson for Not With Our Money.</p><p>The campaign is currently in talks with New York City, Newark, New Jersey and Minneapolis but “Chicago is the first city to take action,” he said.</p><p>According to the campaign’s research team, Chicago currently holds $3.19 billion in contracts with companies that also do business, or have done so, with ICE. The biggest contract is with the infrastructure consultant AECOM, which is overseeing the modernization of O’Hare Airport, according to the group. AECOM's most recent contract with ICE ended last year, according to federal spending records.</p><p>But Bedi said the goal isn’t to nix companies for simply holding a contract with ICE.</p><p>It also requires a company to disclose whether it has been involved in any allegations of excessive force, unlawful detention, unconstitutional policing or discrimination in relation to their government contract, which could then trigger action.</p><p>Johnson and Bedi said the executive order would not apply to the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/25/chicago-parking-meters-deal-stonepeak-ownership-transfer-city-council" > private equity firm Stonepeak </a>that is seeking to take over Chicago’s parking meters from the private company that currently owns them, because the parking meters are “an asset that we completely sold” and have no ownership interest in, Bedi said.</p><p>Stonepeak owns Omni International, an airline company criticized for carrying out deportation flights where detainees were allegedly shackled and denied food and water for more than 10 hours.</p><p>In response to recent news that the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission could stop requiring the collection of demographic data, the order also directs companies making more than $1 billion a year to disclose the composition of their corporate leadership, board of directors and their policies for promoting diversity.</p><p>The state already has a similar requirement for all publicly traded companies headquartered in Illinois with or without state contracts. The executive order would apply to large private companies seeking city business. All companies will also be required to report any efforts to recruit, hire, or promote formerly incarcerated people.</p><p>This is the sixth decree signed by Johnson this year, and the 26th of his term, as he turns to his executive power pen to avoid divisive political battles with a City Council majority that increasingly distrusts Johnson and his legislative efforts.</p><p>And it comes as Johnson prepares to announce whether he’ll run for reelection in a crowded field eager to unseat him.</p><p>“We certainly cannot rely upon a body of government when you have some members who are more interested in protecting the status quo in the interests of corporations,” Johnson said. “I have to do whatever is necessary.”</p>

entries.title: Mega hailstone officially broke state record during 'most severe year for weather in recent memory'
entries.summary: <p>"A real beast" of hail that dropped in Kankakee earlier this year is officially the state's largest recorded hailstone. </p><p>The hailstone — measuring 6.6 inches in diameter and weighing 1.2 pounds — fell into a Kankakee backyard during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/03/11/2-killed-after-storms-bring-at-least-4-twisters-possible-record-setting-hail-in-illinois-and-indiana" target="_blank" >a severe round of storms</a> that also spawned 12 tornadoes back in March. Climatologists with Northern Illinois University <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/03/12/hail-record-size-chicago-illinois-storm-climate-change" target="_blank" >collected the stone</a> and brought it back to their lab to measure and preserve it. </p><p>At the time, meteorologists suspected that the stone handily broke Illinois' previous record-setting stone collected in June 2015 that measured 4.75 inches in diameter.</p><p>On Tuesday, <a class="Link" href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/extremes/scec/reports/20260901-Illinois-Hailstone.pdf" target="_blank" >a report from the State Climate Extremes Committee</a> officially confirmed the new record. That committee assembles whenever a potential record-breaking weather event happens, like after a super cold day or torrential downpour. Committee members include local, regional and national climatologists. </p><p>Trent Ford, the Illinois state climatologist who led the committee, said even though the hail that dropped in March was clearly massive, it's critical to gather experts to go over the evidence before declaring an official record. </p><p>"It may seem like a formality, but it's still an important process to go through," Ford said. "Just because there are pictures of large stones on social media doesn't mean we can simply believe the record was broken." </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Illinois officially has a new state hail record! ⛈️ A colossal hailstone, measuring 6.603 inches in diameter, was confirmed by the SCEC following a storm on March 10, 2026, near Kankakee, IL. It reached historic size, weight, and volume! Learn more: <a href="https://t.co/rToflKSy3q">https://t.co/rToflKSy3q</a> <a href="https://t.co/nukBRD9he3">pic.twitter.com/nukBRD9he3</a></p>— NOAA NCEI (@NOAANCEI) <a href="https://x.com/NOAANCEI/status/2094808359320920122?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 1, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>So far, 2026 has been a banner year for extreme weather in Illinois. Over 200 tornadoes have touched down — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/27/200-tornadoes-illinois-2026" target="_blank" >far surpassing the last record year</a> for twisters. It's also been an especially wet summer with intense flooding. </p><p>"It's probably been the most severe year for weather in recent memory," he said. "Going forward, 2026 will stand out as a record for extreme weather." </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/tornadoes-chicago-what-to-know" >What to know after latest round of tornadoes tear through the Chicago suburbs</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Part of the problem, Ford said, is that climate change is causing heavier rainfall from thunderstorms and generating more intense heat and humidity. </p><p>But it's not as simple to explain the large hailstones and spike in tornadoes. </p><p>"With continuing global warming, it's likely that we could see more conditions that create extreme weather like tornadoes and hail," Ford said. "But the intensity this year is far and away more severe than what we'd see from climate change alone. ... Climate change certainly plays a role, but better research is needed to draw a connection and to see if we can predict whether there will be more severe years." </p><p>There are several key ingredients needed for severe weather. Heat and humidity are some. Big drafts of wind at different speeds and directions also help create the unstable atmosphere for tornadoes and hail, Ford explained. </p><p>"And those ingredients have come together more frequently over Illinois this year, more than any other state," he said. "Why Illinois, why not others? It's all luck." </p><p>Ford acknowledged that luck is an unsatisfying reason. He hopes and expects future research will provide more clarity. </p>
entries.author: Kaitlin Washburn

entries.title: Homewood residents still recovering from storms, hoping for FEMA assistance
entries.summary: <p>Joan Douglas said her 16-year-old daughter was in a bedroom at their Homewood home when a tree branch crashed through the roof during a storm last month.</p><p>Douglas pulled her out and the family rushed to the basement as an EF1 tornado swept through the village on Aug. 11. The 16-year-old was not injured.</p><p>Weeks later, the home remains damaged, with holes in the roof, mold growing inside and branches still scattered across the backyard.</p><p>“We’re trying our best to get things fixed, but we’re struggling,” said Douglas, 38.</p><p>Local, state and federal representatives walked through Douglas’ neighborhood Wednesday morning, speaking with homeowners about the damage their homes sustained during last month’s storms as they gathered information to support a request for relief funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency.</p><p>State officials asked FEMA last week to conduct preliminary damage assessments in the eight counties across Illinois impacted by the storms from Aug. 11-16.</p><p>“We're going to impacted neighborhoods and we're looking to validate the damage that has been reported,” said Kim Keblish, public affairs specialist for FEMA. “So we're looking to have conversations with residents to understand the severity and the magnitude and the impact of these storms.”</p><p>The assessments began Monday and are expected to continue through the rest of the week. Once they are completed, state officials will analyze the data and determine whether federal assistance is needed.</p><p>If they determine it is, Gov. JB Pritzker will request a major disaster declaration and ask the Trump administration for relief funds.</p><p>But there is concern the Trump administration could deny the request, as it has in the past.</p><p>Earlier this year, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/23/disaster-funding-states-lawsuit-trump-conditions-election" target="_blank" >Illinois sued</a> the Trump administration after FEMA denied funding for flood relief in Chicago and the suburbs, where storms last summer caused widespread flooding and overwhelmed sewer systems.</p><div entries.title: Prime Healthcare cuts obstetrics care at 3 Chicago-area hospitals
entries.summary: <p>Prime Healthcare is set to cut obstetrics care at three of its Chicago-area hospitals, the healthcare system announced in a news release.</p><p>OB services will no longer be available at Resurrection Medical Center in Chicago, St. Joseph Medical Center in Joliet and Mercy Medical Center in Aurora, effective Oct. 1.</p><p>The plan is to shift OB services to St. Mary of Nazareth Hospital in Chicago and Olympia Fields Hospital in Olympia Fields and turn its focus to maternal health in the community, according to the news release. Prime will invest $1 million in grant money to initiatives at local nonprofits working to improve maternal health and expand access to prenatal and postpartum care.</p><p>“Concentrating maternity services at established centers like Saint Mary’s ensures the highest levels of quality and patient safety, addressing maternal health disparities,” Dr. Devyani Chawla, director of the Birthing Center at St. Mary of Nazareth, said in the release.</p><p>The three hospitals losing OB services have fewer than one delivery per day, Prime said, and financial woes and changes in ownership made it “impossible to ensure the very best quality of care for the patients served.”</p><p>California-based Prime Healthcare bought nine Illinois Hospitals from Ascension last year, and has been met with skepticism and criticism by employees since. Nurses at St. Mary of Nazareth said conditions at the hospital tanked after Prime bought the hospital, which prompted them to consider unionizing. At least six nurses were fired shortly thereafter.</p><p>“I think it sent a message to the nurses in our community that we’re expendable, and when we speak up for each other, they’ll get rid of us with no just cause,” Karlie Thorn, one of the fired nurses, told the Sun-Times in June.</p><p>Nurses were attempting to unionize with the National Nurses Organizing Committee/National Nurses United, which has criticized the healthcare system heavily. Mariah Robinson, an OB nurse at St. Mary of Nazareth, said the decision to cut OB services is linked to anti-union sentiment from the healthcare system.</p><p>“It's unacceptable that Prime is closing down OB services at other facilities. It's also interesting that this announcement indicates that Prime is closing these services at facilities where nurses are not organized or organizing with our union, NNOC, the most powerful voice for RNs in Illinois and throughout the country,” Robinson said in a statement from NNU. “That said, we will not stop advocating for patients at every hospital where patients are subjected to Prime's and the Reddy Family's greed.”</p>
